additions.source_quote: כִּי שִׂמְחָה הוּא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה מֵרַמַ"ח אֵבָרִים וּשְׁסָ"ה גִּידִים
additions.justification: The text makes an explicit bechina statement: joy (שמחה) IS a complete stature (komah sheleimah) of 248 limbs and 365 sinews. However, the deeper connection to Package 1 is that simcha is the medium through which the nefesh-as-dibur is revealed: when a person passes through the full stature of simcha, the damaged limb (corresponding to the sinned mitzvah) is felt as deagah, which triggers memory of the sin and enables verbal confession. Simcha IS the body/soul-map of all mitzvot. This bechina (simcha = komah sheleimah) does not appear in the Torah #178 dataset. Suggested edge: שמחה ↔ קומה שלמה.

additions.source_quote: כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ נְקֻדּוֹת כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת הִיא הַשִּׂמְחָה, כִּי פִּקּוּדֵי ה' יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי־לֵב
additions.justification: The text states explicitly that the root-point (shoresh nekudot) of all the mitzvot IS simcha — proven from Psalm 19:9: 'The statutes of Hashem are upright, rejoicing the heart.' This is a bechina statement: the essential inner point (nekudah) of every commandment IS joy. Each of the 613 mitzvot has a corresponding limb in the stature of simcha. This concept — that simcha is the essential nature of Torah observance — is central to the Torah's argument but does not appear as a bechina node for Torah #178 in the dataset. Suggested edge: שרש נקודות המצוות ↔ שמחה.

additions.source_quote: וְאַדְּרַבָּא, יֵשׁ לוֹ דְּאָגָה, שֶׁהוּא הֶפֶךְ הַשִּׂמְחָה, בִּבְחִינַת אֶדְאַג מֵחַטָּאתִי
additions.justification: The text states explicitly: 'there is deagah (worry), which is the OPPOSITE of simcha (שֶׁהוּא הֶפֶךְ הַשִּׂמְחָה).' This is a bechina-of-opposition: deagah IS the inverse nature of simcha. In the Torah's structure, deagah functions as the signal that appears at the damaged mitzvah-limb when the simcha stature passes over it — it IS the manifestation of the sin's damage in the nefesh domain. Deagah is the evil mirror of simcha in this Torah: where simcha IS the body of holiness (komah sheleimah), deagah IS the disruption/damage. Suggested edge: דאגה ↔ חטא (or דאגה ↔ פגם המצוה). This would be an evil-polarity bechina node.

additions.source_quote: נִתְעוֹרֵר הַקּוֹל דִּלְעֵלָּא וְנִתְיַחֵד עִם הַדִּבּוּר
additions.justification: The text describes the kol (voice from above) as the complementary dimension to dibur (speech from below): 'the upper kol is awakened and desires to unite with dibur.' The relationship between kol and dibur in this Torah is presented as a yichud (union of two that share an essential complementarity). While the immediate framing is that repairing dibur CAUSES the awakening of kol (eitza), the text also frames kol and dibur as two halves of a single reality — the divine voice needing the human word to complete itself. The verse 'osei devaro lishmo'a bekol devaro' is interpreted as: those who do (= repair) dibur merit to hear (= receive) kol. However, this relationship may be best classified as eitza rather than bechina in the Torah's logic. Flagged here for human review.

additions.source_quote: וְעַל יְדֵי וִדּוּי דְּבָרִים נִתְתַּקֵּן עוֹלַם הַדִּבּוּר
additions.justification: Viduy devarim (verbal confession) is described as the specific repair action for dibur (speech). In the Torah's language, the sin causes damage to the nefesh=dibur, and the repair IS viduy devarim. This could be read as eitza (viduy REPAIRS dibur), but the Torah frames them as sharing the same essential domain: the world of speech (olam hadibur) is what is damaged and what is repaired, and viduy IS speech by definition. The citation of Hosea 14:3 — 'Take words with you and return to Hashem' — suggests that viduy IS the expression of the nefesh-as-dibur repairing itself. This is more naturally eitza, but if read as bechina: viduy IS the active form of the repaired dibur. Flagged for human review.

analysis_notes.note_on_sparse_bechina_coverage: Torah #178 is notably sparse in the bechina dataset — only 1 edge is recorded. This stands in sharp contrast to the teaching's rich conceptual content. The reason is that the Torah's argument is structured almost entirely as an eitza chain: simcha of mitzvah → enables passing through the full komah → reveals the damaged limb → triggers deagah → triggers memory of sin → enables viduy → repairs dibur → causes yichud of kol and dibur. The only bechina in this chain that the encoder identified is the foundational identity: nefesh=dibur. All other relationships are cause-and-effect (eitza). The gap analysis above identifies several additional bechina identities present in the text that were not captured.
analysis_notes.note_on_evil_mirror: The evil mirror in Torah #178 is subtle: simcha (good) ↔ deagah (evil); komah sheleimah (good) ↔ the damaged limb/sin-laden body (evil); dibur repaired (good) ↔ dibur damaged by sin (evil). The Torah does not develop the evil side as an independent cluster — it focuses almost entirely on the positive path of repair. The evil dimension appears as the starting problem (sin, obstacles to confession, worry) rather than as an independent conceptual domain.
